newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY HIGH COURT CONVICTS 3 OF 1956 KILLINGS.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY HIGH COURT CONVICTS 3 OF 1956 KILLINGS.

text.p: The Supreme Court, Hungary's ultimate court of appeal, ruled on Thursday that three men were guilty of committing crimes against humanity for helping suppress the 1956 anti-communist uprising, the MTI news agency reported.
The ruling marked the first time prosecution managed to bring convictions to their final judicial stage in their drawn-out struggle to put totalitarianism's henchmen behind bars.
The court ruled that the Budapest Municipal Court was correct when in January, 1995, it found Lajos Orosz guilty of having committed crimes against humanity, but was wrong in convicting Ferenc Toldi.

The two, as well as 10 others who were acquitted, were accused of being part of a pro-communist militia that fired on demonstrators on December 8, 1956 in Salgotarjan, a small northern mining town, killing 47 people and injuring up to 89.
The Supreme Court overturned two of the 1995 acquittals, sentencing Nandor Levardi and Ferenc Szoboszlai to two years each which Szoboszlai will not have to serve under a 1990 amnesty, MTI said.

The Salgotarjan case was the first crimes against humanity trial. Five of six other prosecutions resulted in acquittals while last month, the Supreme Court overturned the convictions of two men in the sixth case, ordering a new trial.
Hungary began prosecuting people who brutally suppressed their countrymen under communism after a 1993 Constitutional Court ruling that said crimes against humanity do not have a limitation period.
All the prosecutions involved relatively law-rank members of militias who served as the stormtroops of the communist government that suppressed a short-lived democracy in 1956 with Soviet help.
